questions.stem: A 21 year old woman has a 2 month history of aching hands, tiredness and painless ulcers on the roof of her mouth. After a beach holiday a red rash appeared across both cheeks and the bridge of her nose. The skin of the nasolabial folds is spared. Her wrists and finger joints are tender on both sides but there is no deformity. Her temperature is 37.4°C and pulse rate 88 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A young woman with a photosensitive malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds, oral ulcers and symmetrical arthralgia has SLE. Lupus pernio in sarcoidosis is the classic misnomer distractor.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: painless ulcers on the roof of her mouth
steps.x: Young woman, **photosensitive malar rash** sparing the nasolabial folds, mouth ulcers and symmetrical joint tenderness: a multisystem autoimmune picture.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Systemic lupus erythematosus.

elim: The facial rash is heliotrope around the eyes with proximal muscle weakness and Gottron's papules.
Gives symmetrical small joint synovitis but not a photosensitive malar rash or mouth ulcers.
Causes facial flushing and pustules in middle age; no arthritis or oral ulcers.
Lupus pernio is a purple nasal rash in sarcoid; expect hilar nodes and erythema nodosum.

steps.x: **E. Systemic lupus erythematosus.** Malar rash + oral ulcers + arthralgia in a young woman = SLE until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has had painful, stiff hands for 4 months. The pain affects the wrists and metacarpophalangeal joints on both sides equally. The joints are tender with mild soft tissue swelling but there is no fixed deformity. She takes hydroxychloroquine. Her temperature is 36.9°C. X-rays of both hands are taken.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on the hand X-rays?
o: Juxta-articular erosions with joint space loss
Osteophytes at the distal interphalangeal joints
questions.e: Lupus arthritis is symmetrical but non-erosive, so the X-rays are usually normal. Erosions point to rheumatoid arthritis.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Known SLE with **symmetrical** small joint pain and **no deformity**: lupus arthritis is mild and **non-erosive**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: No erosions.

elim: These are the erosive changes of rheumatoid arthritis, not lupus arthritis.
Osteophytes and Heberden's nodes are osteoarthritis.
Classic of psoriatic arthritis mutilans.
Typical of chronic tophaceous gout.

steps.x: **B. No erosions.** SLE arthritis = symmetrical, non-erosive; erosions mean think again (RA).

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has 3 days of sharp central chest pain that is worse lying flat and eased by sitting forward. She also has a flare of her facial rash. A scratchy sound is heard at the left sternal edge. Her temperature is 37.5°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. ECG (see item resources).

visual.title: 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: Widespread saddle-shaped ST elevation without reciprocal change: pericarditis.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Positional chest pain eased by sitting forward with a rub and widespread ST elevation is pericarditis; in a lupus flare this is serositis, one of the classification criteria.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Positional pain, **pericardial rub** and widespread ST elevation during a flare: **serositis**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Lupus pericarditis.

elim: Would give regional ST elevation with reciprocal change, not widespread saddle ST elevation eased by sitting forward.
Tearing pain radiating to the back with BP difference between arms.
Reproducible chest wall tenderness; no rub or ECG change.
Pleuritic pain with hypoxia and tachypnoea; no friction rub or positional relief.

steps.x: **D. Lupus pericarditis.** Serositis (pericarditis or pleuritis) is a classic SLE feature and an ARA criterion.

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman has a 1 year history of red, scaly patches on her cheeks, ears and scalp. The lesions are worse in summer and some have healed leaving pale scars and patches of permanent hair loss. She has no joint pain, mouth ulcers or fatigue. Her full blood count, urine dipstick and complement levels are normal and her antinuclear antibody is negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Red scaling plaques on sun-exposed skin that scar, in a woman with no systemic features and negative ANA, is chronic discoid lupus. SLE needs multisystem involvement.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: no joint pain, mouth ulcers or fatigue
steps.x: **Scarring red scaly plaques** in sun-exposed skin with **no systemic disease**: skin-limited lupus.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Chronic discoid lupus erythematosus.

elim: Rough small lesions on sun-damaged skin in older people, without scarring alopecia.
Silvery plaques on extensor surfaces; does not scar or worsen with sun.
She has no systemic features, normal bloods and a negative ANA.
Fungal scalp infection, usually in children, with scaling and broken hairs.

steps.x: **B. Chronic discoid lupus erythematosus.** Discoid lupus = scarring photosensitive plaques, skin only, commonest in women.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man has 2 months of aching joints, muscle pain and sharp left-sided chest pain on breathing in. He started hydralazine for hypertension 6 months ago. He has no rash, his urine dipstick is negative and his creatinine is normal. His temperature is 37.6°C. His antinuclear antibody is positive. A further antibody is requested.
questions.q: Which antibody is most likely to be positive?
questions.e: Arthralgia, myalgia and serositis without renal or CNS disease after starting hydralazine is drug-induced lupus, marked by anti-histone antibodies.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: sharp left-sided chest pain on breathing in
steps.x: Older man, **new drug (hydralazine)**, arthralgia, myalgia and pleurisy, **kidneys spared**: drug-induced lupus.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Anti-histone antibodies.

elim: Associated with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis.
Specific for rheumatoid arthritis.
Seen in polymyositis with interstitial lung disease.
Highly specific for idiopathic SLE, which is unlikely in an older man on hydralazine.

steps.x: **C. Anti-histone antibodies.** Drug-induced lupus = anti-histone antibodies; no renal or CNS disease.

questions.stem: A 35 year old woman is on treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis with rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol. Four months in she develops painful joints, aching muscles and pleuritic chest pain. Her urine dipstick is normal. Her antinuclear and anti-histone antibodies are positive and her anti-dsDNA is negative. Her temperature is 37.3°C and BP 116/72 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Stop all TB treatment for 6 months
Stop isoniazid under TB specialist advice
questions.e: Anti-histone positive, anti-dsDNA negative lupus while on isoniazid is drug-induced lupus, which resolves on stopping the drug. TB therapy is continued with a substitute.

steps.x: It asks for a management step: decide how unwell the patient is and what comes first.
Lupus-like illness after **isoniazid** with **anti-histone** antibodies and spared kidneys.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Stop isoniazid under TB specialist advice.

elim: Immunosuppression is not needed; the condition resolves when the drug is stopped.
Reserved for organ-threatening SLE; she has no renal or CNS disease.
First-line for idiopathic SLE, not for a drug-induced reaction.
Stopping all treatment risks relapse and resistance; only the culprit drug is changed.

steps.x: **E. Stop isoniazid under TB specialist advice.** Drug-induced lupus: stop the culprit drug and it resolves.

questions.stem: A 23 year old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus is brought in by her partner. For 4 days she has had a severe headache and says strangers are reading her thoughts. She takes only hydroxychloroquine and has never used recreational drugs. She has a florid malar rash. Her temperature is 37.2°C. Her C3 is low and anti-dsDNA titre has risen. CT head is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
questions.e: Psychosis and severe headache with a malar rash, low C3 and rising anti-dsDNA is cerebral (neuropsychiatric) lupus.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
**Psychosis + severe headache** in active SLE (low C3, rising anti-dsDNA): the brain is involved.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Neuropsychiatric lupus.

elim: She is not taking steroids.
Causes retinopathy, not acute psychosis with a disease flare.
A first psychosis with headache during a clear lupus flare is organic until proven otherwise.
Thunderclap headache with meningism; CT head is normal and psychosis is not typical.

steps.x: **C. Neuropsychiatric lupus.** Cerebral lupus = psychosis and severe headache with the malar rash.

questions.stem: A baby boy is born at 38 weeks. A slow fetal heart rate was first noticed at 22 weeks. His mother has fatigue, dry eyes and a photosensitive rash, and has never been investigated. The baby's pulse rate is 52 bpm and he has a faint red rash around the eyes. ECG (see item resources).

visual.title: Neonatal rhythm strip
visual.caption: P waves march through with no relation to the slow broad QRS complexes: complete heart block.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Neonatal lupus with congenital heart block
questions.e: Complete heart block found from mid-pregnancy with a neonatal rash, in a mother with photosensitive rash and sicca symptoms, is neonatal lupus from anti-Ro/anti-La antibodies.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Fetal bradycardia from **18 to 28 weeks**, a **complete heart block** ECG and maternal photosensitive rash.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Neonatal lupus with congenital heart block.

elim: Gives prolonged QT and torsades, not AV dissociation with a maternal rash.
Causes bradycardia acutely in labour, not a persistent slow rate from 22 weeks.
Causes mild bradycardia with jaundice and poor feeding, not complete heart block.
P waves would conduct to every QRS; here they are dissociated.

steps.x: **D. Neonatal lupus with congenital heart block.** Neonatal lupus: transplacental anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB cause congenital heart block.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus is 20 weeks pregnant. Her fetal heart rate is 60 bpm on routine scan. Fetal echocardiography shows atrioventricular dissociation with normal cardiac structure. Her anti-Ro (SSA) and anti-La (SSB) antibodies are positive.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the fetal heart rhythm?
o: Maternal anti-dsDNA damaging the fetal myocardium
Maternal antibodies cause inflammation and fibrosis of the fetal AV node
questions.e: IgG anti-Ro and anti-La cross the placenta, bind fetal conduction tissue and cause AV node inflammation and fibrosis, giving congenital heart block.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: link the finding in the stem to the underlying biology.
Mid-pregnancy **AV dissociation** with normal structure and **anti-Ro/La** positive mother.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Maternal antibodies cause inflammation and fibrosis of the fetal AV node.

elim: Causes variable decelerations, not fixed AV dissociation with a normal heart.
Hydroxychloroquine is safe in pregnancy and does not cause heart block.
Anti-dsDNA is linked to nephritis, not fetal conduction disease.
Echocardiography shows normal structure.

steps.x: **D. Maternal antibodies cause inflammation and fibrosis of the fetal AV node.** Anti-Ro/La cross the placenta and scar the fetal AV node.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has 2 weeks of tiredness, breathlessness on stairs and yellow eyes. Her conjunctivae are pale and her sclerae are icteric. Her pulse rate is 106 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely additional finding?
o: Schistocytes with a negative Coombs test
questions.e: Anaemia with jaundice in SLE suggests autoimmune haemolytic anaemia: low Hb, raised LDH and a positive direct antiglobulin test.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Anaemia **plus jaundice** in SLE: red cells are being destroyed by autoantibodies.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Positive direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test.

elim: LDH is raised, not low, when red cells are destroyed.
The marrow responds to haemolysis with a high reticulocyte count.
Haptoglobin is used up and falls in haemolysis.
Fragmented cells suggest microangiopathy, not antibody-mediated haemolysis.

steps.x: **C. Positive direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test.** AIHA in SLE = low Hb, high LDH, DAT positive.

questions.stem: A 25 year old woman has 3 months of fatigue, painful wrists, patchy hair loss and a facial rash after sun exposure. Her temperature is 37.4°C. Her antinuclear antibody is strongly positive and anti-dsDNA is positive. A full blood count is taken.
questions.q: Which is the most likely full blood count finding?
questions.e: Active SLE typically causes cytopenias, especially lymphopenia and thrombocytopenia, alongside low C3 and C4.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Clear SLE picture: expect **cytopenias**, not raised counts.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Lymphopenia.

elim: Suggests allergy, parasites or eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
Points to bacterial infection or steroid use, not active lupus.
Not a feature of SLE; anaemia is more likely.
Lupus lowers platelets; a high count suggests another inflammatory process.

steps.x: **B. Lymphopenia.** SLE bloods: lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia, low C3/C4.

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus attends clinic with puffy eyelids and ankle swelling for 10 days. Her urine looks dark. Her BP is 162/98 mmHg and pulse rate 84 bpm. She has pitting oedema to the shins. Her creatinine has risen from 68 to 124 µmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on urine dipstick?
questions.e: Oedema, hypertension, dark urine and rising creatinine in SLE is lupus nephritis, with proteinuria and haematuria on dipstick.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Nephritic features (**hypertension, dark urine, rising creatinine**) in SLE: glomerular inflammation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Blood and protein.

elim: Glycosuria suggests diabetes or proximal tubular disease.
Suggest urinary tract infection, not glomerular disease.
Hypertension, oedema and rising creatinine in SLE point to nephritis.
Pure proteinuria fits nephrotic minimal change; dark urine and hypertension mean blood is present too.

steps.x: **A. Blood and protein.** Lupus nephritis = proteinuria and haematuria on dipstick.

questions.stem: A 41 year old woman has had systemic lupus erythematosus for 18 years. She has 40 minutes of central crushing chest pain radiating to her left arm. She does not smoke and has no family history of heart disease. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 138/86 mmHg. ECG (see item resources).

visual.title: 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: ST elevation V1 to V4 with inferior reciprocal depression: anterior STEMI.

questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her chest pain?
o: Myocardial infarction from premature coronary artery disease
questions.e: Long-standing SLE accelerates atherosclerosis, so young women with lupus get premature coronary artery disease. Regional anterior ST elevation is a STEMI, not pericarditis.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
**Crushing** pain with **regional** anterior ST elevation in a young woman with long-standing SLE.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Myocardial infarction from premature coronary artery disease.

elim: Tearing back pain; the ECG shows a regional infarct pattern.
Gives widespread saddle ST elevation eased by sitting forward, not anterior ST elevation with crushing pain.
Can mimic angina but does not cause regional ST elevation.
Pleuritic pain and hypoxia; ST elevation in V1 to V4 points to the LAD.

steps.x: **C. Myocardial infarction from premature coronary artery disease.** SLE is a coronary risk factor: think premature CAD in young lupus patients with chest pain.

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has a renal biopsy for proteinuria. Microscopy shows granular deposits of antibody bound to DNA along the glomerular basement membrane, with complement activation and neutrophil infiltration. Similar deposits are found at the dermal-epidermal junction of her skin.
questions.q: Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is most likely responsible?
questions.e: SLE is a type III reaction: circulating antigen-antibody (e.g. anti-dsDNA) complexes deposit in the GBM and skin, activate complement and cause local inflammation.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: link the finding in the stem to the underlying biology.

clues: granular deposits of antibody bound to DNA
steps.x: **Granular** deposits of **antigen-antibody complexes** in more than one tissue, activating complement.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Type III hypersensitivity.

elim: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation, as in anaphylaxis.
Antibodies bind fixed antigens on cells, giving linear deposits (e.g. Goodpasture).
T-cell mediated and delayed, with no antibody deposits.
Antibodies stimulate a receptor, as in Graves' disease.

steps.x: **C. Type III hypersensitivity.** SLE = type III, immune complex hypersensitivity.

questions.stem: A 19 year old woman has 6 weeks of fever, muscle aches and joint pains in her hands and knees. She has noticed clumps of hair on her pillow and painless ulcers inside her nose. She has small rubbery nodes in her neck and armpits. Her temperature is 37.8°C. Her platelet count is 88 ×10⁹/L and lymphocytes 0.6 ×10⁹/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Young woman with fever, myalgia, arthralgia, alopecia, painless nasal ulcers, lymphadenopathy, lymphopenia and thrombocytopenia: a multisystem picture of SLE.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
**Alopecia, mucosal ulcers, arthralgia, lymphadenopathy and cytopenias** together in a young woman.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Systemic lupus erythematosus.

elim: Painful oral and genital ulcers with uveitis; alopecia and cytopenias are not typical.
Painless nodes with B symptoms, but not nasal ulcers, alopecia and arthralgia.
Tender nodes, sore throat and atypical lymphocytosis rather than lymphopenia.
Asymmetrical large joint arthritis after infection, with urethritis or conjunctivitis.

steps.x: **E. Systemic lupus erythematosus.** Many systems + young woman + cytopenias = think SLE.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman has ring-shaped red scaly patches on her upper back, chest and forearms that appear every summer and heal without scarring. She also has mild joint aches and dry eyes. Her antinuclear antibody is positive. Her platelet count is 110 ×10⁹/L. A further antibody test is requested.
questions.q: Which antibody is most likely to be positive?
questions.e: Photosensitive annular non-scarring plaques are subacute cutaneous lupus; anti-Ro is linked to photosensitive rashes, subacute cutaneous lupus and cytopenias.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.
**Photosensitive, annular, non-scarring** rash with a low platelet count: subacute cutaneous lupus.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Anti-Ro (SSA).

elim: Linked to limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis with calcinosis and Raynaud's.
Marker of drug-induced lupus; she takes no causative drug.
Marker of primary biliary cholangitis.
Linked to diffuse systemic sclerosis.

steps.x: **D. Anti-Ro (SSA).** Anti-Ro = photosensitive rash, SCLE, cytopenias, neonatal lupus.

questions.stem: A 28 year old woman is newly diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus in rheumatology clinic. She has a malar rash and arthralgia. She feels otherwise well and has no swelling. Her BP is 124/78 mmHg. The consultant wants to look for kidney involvement today.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: Every patient with SLE should have a urine dipstick for proteinuria and haematuria to look for lupus nephritis; biopsy comes later if it is abnormal.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.

clues: newly diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus
steps.x: Screening a **new SLE patient** for **nephritis** at the bedside.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Urine dipstick.

elim: Quantifies protein later, but is not the first bedside screen.
Gives anatomy, not glomerular inflammation.
Confirms and classifies nephritis once dipstick and blood tests suggest it.
Shows kidney size and obstruction, not early glomerulonephritis.

steps.x: **E. Urine dipstick.** First-line in all SLE: urine dipstick for protein (and blood).

questions.stem: A 32 year old woman has 3 months of tiredness and aching knees and hands. She read online that she may have lupus. Her examination is normal with no rash or synovitis. Her temperature is 36.8°C. Her full blood count, ESR, urine dipstick and C3 are normal and her antinuclear antibody is negative.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate interpretation of the antinuclear antibody result?
o: A specific antibody is still needed to exclude SLE
The test should be repeated weekly
questions.e: ANA is positive in over 95% of SLE, so a negative result makes SLE very unlikely; it is a sensitive rule-out test.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.
Normal examination and bloods with a **negative ANA**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: SLE is very unlikely.

elim: ANA is the sensitive rule-out test; specific antibodies are for confirming, not excluding.
Drug-induced lupus is also ANA positive, with anti-histone antibodies.
A negative ANA cannot confirm SLE.
Repeat testing without new features adds nothing.

steps.x: **D. SLE is very unlikely.** ANA = sensitive, rules out; anti-dsDNA/anti-Smith = specific, rule in.

questions.stem: A 22 year old woman has a photosensitive facial rash, mouth ulcers and painful wrists. Her antinuclear antibody is positive at 1:640. The rheumatologist wants a test that is highly specific for systemic lupus erythematosus to confirm the diagnosis. Her anti-dsDNA result is awaited.
questions.q: Which other antibody is the most specific for this condition?
questions.e: ANA is sensitive but not specific; anti-Smith and anti-dsDNA are the most specific antibodies for SLE.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.
ANA is positive, now a **specific** test is needed besides anti-dsDNA.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Anti-Smith.

elim: Points to limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis.
Specific for rheumatoid arthritis.
Seen in inflammatory myositis with lung disease.
Neither sensitive nor specific; positive in many conditions.

steps.x: **D. Anti-Smith.** Most specific for SLE: anti-Smith and anti-dsDNA.

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has haematuria, proteinuria of 2.8 g per day and a creatinine of 142 µmol/L. Her BP is 150/94 mmHg and she has ankle oedema. Her C3 is low. Ultrasound shows two normal-sized kidneys. A renal biopsy is performed and sent for immunofluorescence.
questions.q: Which is the most likely immunofluorescence finding?
o: Deposits of IgG, IgA, IgM, C3 and C1q
Linear IgG along the basement membrane
questions.e: Lupus nephritis gives a 'full house' pattern: IgG, IgA, IgM, C3 and C1q all positive.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.
Biopsy of **lupus nephritis**: immune complexes of every class plus complement.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Deposits of IgG, IgA, IgM, C3 and C1q.

elim: Linear staining is anti-GBM (Goodpasture) disease.
Typical of IgA nephropathy.
Pauci-immune staining points to ANCA vasculitis.
Seen in post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

steps.x: **A. Deposits of IgG, IgA, IgM, C3 and C1q.** Lupus nephritis biopsy = 'full house' immunofluorescence.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has 3 days of fever, cough and green sputum. She takes azathioprine and hydroxychloroquine. Her rash and joints are unchanged. Her temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute. Investigations show CRP 168 mg/L (<5), ESR 24 mm/h (<20), normal C3 and stable anti-dsDNA.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation of the raised CRP?
questions.e: In SLE the ESR rises with disease activity but the CRP usually does not, so a high CRP with stable complement points to infection, likely a chest infection on azathioprine.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.
**Very high CRP** with **normal C3** and stable anti-dsDNA in an immunosuppressed patient with sputum.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Infection.

elim: Does not cause fever or a high CRP.
Flares raise ESR and lower complement while CRP stays low; her C3 and anti-dsDNA are stable.
Would cause proteinuria and haematuria, not productive cough and high CRP.
Lupus serositis can raise CRP a little, but she has fever and green sputum on immunosuppression.

steps.x: **B. Infection.** In SLE: high CRP = think infection; high ESR + low C3 = think flare.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus is reviewed in clinic. Over 2 weeks her rash and joint pains have worsened and she is more tired. Her temperature is 37.3°C. Several blood results are available and the team wants to know if her disease is active.
questions.q: Which result most suggests active disease?
questions.e: Active immune complex formation consumes complement, so low C3 and C4 correlate with disease activity, alongside a high ESR and rising anti-dsDNA.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.

clues: rash and joint pains have worsened
steps.x: Monitoring **activity**: which marker moves with immune complex formation?

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Low C3.

elim: ESR rises with disease activity; a falling ESR suggests improvement.
A rising anti-dsDNA titre tracks activity; negative is reassuring.
Complement is consumed and falls in active disease.
A liver or bone marker, not a lupus activity marker.

steps.x: **B. Low C3.** Lower C3/C4 = higher activity (complement consumption).

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman is diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus. Her antinuclear, anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith antibodies are all positive. Her C3 and C4 are low and she has a malar rash, mouth ulcers and arthralgia. She has no recent infection and takes no regular medicines. She asks why her immune system is making antibodies against her own cells.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of autoantibody production?
o: Loss of tolerance to nuclear antigens
Molecular mimicry with streptococcal M protein
questions.e: In SLE self-tolerance to nuclear antigens is lost, so B cells make ANA and more specific antibodies such as anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: link the finding in the stem to the underlying biology.
All three antibodies are against **nuclear** material.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Loss of tolerance to nuclear antigens.

elim: Type V receptor-stimulating antibodies, as in Graves' disease.
Type I allergy, not autoantibody formation.
The mechanism of rheumatic fever.
Type IV, as in sarcoidosis or TB.

steps.x: **C. Loss of tolerance to nuclear antigens.** SLE autoantibodies come from loss of tolerance to nuclear antigens.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man with arrhythmia has taken procainamide for a year. He develops joint pains, muscle aches and pleuritic chest pain. His urine dipstick, creatinine and neurological examination are normal. His antinuclear and anti-histone antibodies are positive. His symptoms settle after the drug is stopped.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his illness?
o: Deposition of drug-antibody complexes in the glomeruli
Drug-induced modification of histones that become antigenic
Loss of tolerance to double-stranded DNA
questions.e: Drugs such as procainamide, hydralazine and isoniazid modify histones so they become antigenic, generating anti-histone antibodies without the renal and CNS disease of idiopathic SLE.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: link the finding in the stem to the underlying biology.

clues: urine dipstick, creatinine and neurological examination are normal
settle after the drug is stopped
steps.x: A drug, **anti-histone** antibodies, **no renal or CNS disease** and recovery on stopping.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Drug-induced modification of histones that become antigenic.

elim: Drug-induced lupus spares the kidneys; his renal tests are normal.
Would not produce ANA and anti-histone antibodies.
Causes urticaria and anaphylaxis, not a lupus-like syndrome.
Idiopathic SLE mechanism with renal and CNS disease.

steps.x: **C. Drug-induced modification of histones that become antigenic.** Drug-induced lupus: altered histones become antigens.

questions.stem: A 22 year old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has new haematuria with red cell casts, proteinuria and a BP of 158/96 mmHg. Her C3 and C4 are low and anti-dsDNA titre is high. Renal biopsy shows increased cellularity of the glomeruli.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her renal disease?
o: Anti-GBM antibodies binding type IV collagen
Immune complex deposition along the glomerular basement membrane causing proliferative glomerulonephritis
questions.e: Anti-dsDNA immune complexes deposit along the GBM, activate complement (low C3/C4) and cause a proliferative glomerulonephritis with nephritic features.

steps.x: It asks for a mechanism: link the finding in the stem to the underlying biology.
**Low complement**, high anti-dsDNA and a **proliferative** glomerular picture.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Immune complex deposition along the glomerular basement membrane causing proliferative glomerulonephritis.

elim: Pauci-immune; complement is usually normal.
Goodpasture disease, with linear staining.
Hydroxychloroquine does not cause glomerulonephritis.
Minimal change disease, with no haematuria or casts.

steps.x: **D. Immune complex deposition along the glomerular basement membrane causing proliferative glomerulonephritis.** Lupus nephritis = immune complexes on the GBM, complement activation, proliferative GN.

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman with mild systemic lupus erythematosus affecting skin and joints is started on long-term treatment. Her BP is 118/72 mmHg, urine dipstick is negative and full blood count is normal. She asks which side effect she should know about with her new tablet, which is the first-line disease-modifying drug for her condition.
questions.q: Which adverse effect is most important to monitor for?
questions.e: Hydroxychloroquine is the first-line DMARD for mild SLE; its key adverse effect is retinal toxicity causing irreversible vision loss, so eyes are screened.

steps.x: It asks for a management step: decide how unwell the patient is and what comes first.
Mild SLE first-line DMARD is **hydroxychloroquine**: what does it damage?

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Irreversible retinal toxicity.

elim: An adverse effect of cyclophosphamide.
More relevant to methotrexate.
Seen with aminoglycosides, not hydroxychloroquine.
Linked to methotrexate and amiodarone.

steps.x: **C. Irreversible retinal toxicity.** Hydroxychloroquine: retinopathy, irreversible, needs eye screening.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has ongoing arthritis and rash despite 6 months of hydroxychloroquine. The rheumatologist decides to add the usual second-line immunosuppressive drug, a purine analogue. Her urine dipstick is negative and full blood count normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation before starting the new drug?
questions.e: Second-line in SLE is azathioprine. Low TPMT activity causes severe myelosuppression, so TPMT is checked before starting (standard UK practice).

steps.x: It asks for a management step: decide how unwell the patient is and what comes first.
Second-line after hydroxychloroquine is **azathioprine**: check the enzyme that breaks it down.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) activity.

elim: Tracks lupus activity but does not affect safety of the new drug.
Not needed before thiopurine therapy.
Done before methotrexate in some patients, not azathioprine.
Screens for hydroxychloroquine retinopathy, not thiopurine toxicity.

steps.x: **D. Thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) activity.** Azathioprine is second-line; check TPMT first.

questions.stem: A 25 year old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has 3 weeks of frothy urine and leg swelling. Her BP is 164/100 mmHg. Her creatinine has risen from 70 to 168 µmol/L and urine protein:creatinine ratio is 380 mg/mmol. Renal biopsy shows diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Lupus nephritis needs high-dose corticosteroids with a cytotoxic drug: cyclophosphamide, or mycophenolate mofetil or tacrolimus as alternatives.

steps.x: It asks for a management step: decide how unwell the patient is and what comes first.
**Biopsy-proven proliferative nephritis** with rising creatinine: organ-threatening.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: High-dose corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide.

elim: Mild disease treatment; inadequate for organ-threatening nephritis.
Too low a dose and no cytotoxic agent.
Used for anti-GBM disease, not first-line for lupus nephritis.
Helps proteinuria but does not treat the active nephritis.

steps.x: **A. High-dose corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide.** Lupus nephritis: high-dose steroids + cytotoxic (cyclophosphamide, mycophenolate or tacrolimus).

questions.stem: A 20 year old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has a generalised seizure and is hallucinating. Her malar rash has flared. Her temperature is 37.4°C. CT head, lumbar puncture and blood glucose are normal and infection has been excluded. Her C3 is low. She has been given intravenous methylprednisolone.
questions.q: Which drug should be added?
questions.e: Cerebral lupus is treated with high-dose corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide once infection is excluded.

steps.x: It asks for a management step: decide how unwell the patient is and what comes first.
Seizure and psychosis in a lupus flare after **infection is excluded**: severe neurological lupus.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Cyclophosphamide.

elim: Second-line maintenance agent; too slow for severe cerebral disease.
First-line for mild disease; not enough for cerebral lupus.
Steroid-sparing for joints and skin, not induction for CNS lupus.
Controls seizures but does not treat the underlying cerebral lupus.

steps.x: **B. Cyclophosphamide.** Cerebral lupus: high-dose steroids + cyclophosphamide.

questions.stem: A 28 year old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has 2 days of nosebleeds and a widespread petechial rash. She is alert. Her pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg. Investigations show platelets 9 ×10⁹/L (150–400), haemoglobin 128 g/L and normal clotting.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Watch and repeat the count in a week
questions.e: A severe haematological flare (bleeding with platelets 9) needs high-dose corticosteroids first; cyclophosphamide may follow for serious disease.

steps.x: It asks for a management step: decide how unwell the patient is and what comes first.
**Bleeding** with a **very low platelet count** in SLE: a severe haematological flare.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: High-dose corticosteroids.

elim: Too slow for a dangerous haematological flare.
Antiplatelet treatment would worsen bleeding.
A last resort for refractory thrombocytopenia, not initial care.
A platelet count of 9 with bleeding needs urgent treatment.

steps.x: **A. High-dose corticosteroids.** Severe flare: high-dose prednisolone (± cyclophosphamide).

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus takes hydroxychloroquine. After a stressful month she has 1 week of worsening joint pain, a flare of her malar rash and tiredness. Her temperature is 37.3°C and BP 120/78 mmHg. Her urine dipstick is negative and full blood count is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: A flare without organ-threatening disease is treated with corticosteroids (prednisolone) while continuing hydroxychloroquine.

steps.x: It asks for a management step: decide how unwell the patient is and what comes first.
A **skin and joint flare** with no renal, CNS or blood involvement.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Short course of oral prednisolone.

elim: Reserved for severe renal, neurological or haematological flares.
A specialist option for refractory disease, not a mild flare.
It should be continued; stopping it increases flares.
Will not settle a flare with joint pain and rash.

steps.x: **C. Short course of oral prednisolone.** SLE flare: corticosteroids (prednisolone); keep the hydroxychloroquine going.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has 1 week of sharp pain in both sides of her chest on deep breathing and mild breathlessness. She has no cough or sputum and has not travelled. Her temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 92 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. Chest X-ray (see item resources).

visual.title: Chest X-ray
visual.caption: Small bilateral pleural effusions blunting both costophrenic angles.

questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her chest X-ray findings?
questions.e: Bilateral pleuritic pain with small bilateral effusions in SLE is pleuritis, part of the serositis criterion.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: sharp pain in both sides of her chest on deep breathing
steps.x: **Bilateral pleuritic pain**, small effusions, no infection: lupus pleuritis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Lupus serositis.

elim: Would give fever, productive cough and consolidation.
Effusions with cardiomegaly and pulmonary oedema in an older patient.
Usually a normal X-ray with hypoxia; bilateral effusions with pleuritic pain point to pleuritis.
Gives upper zone cavitation with weight loss and night sweats.

steps.x: **C. Lupus serositis.** Serositis (pleuritis/pericarditis) is classic SLE.

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman is referred with fatigue and joint pains. She says her face goes red every time she is in the sun. Her temperature is 37.2°C. Her antinuclear and anti-dsDNA antibodies are positive. The doctor examines her face.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of her face?
o: Erythema over the cheeks sparing the nasolabial folds
Silvery scaling plaques on the hairline
questions.e: The malar (butterfly) rash of SLE lies over the cheeks and nasal bridge, spares the nasolabial folds and is photosensitive.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: face goes red every time she is in the sun
antinuclear and anti-dsDNA antibodies are positive
steps.x: **Photosensitive** facial redness with positive ANA and anti-dsDNA.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Erythema over the cheeks sparing the nasolabial folds.

elim: Dermatomyositis, with proximal weakness.
Rosacea.
Lupus pernio, a feature of sarcoidosis despite the name.
Psoriasis.

steps.x: **A. Erythema over the cheeks sparing the nasolabial folds.** Malar rash spares the nasolabial folds and is worse with sunlight.

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has 1 week of easy bruising and bleeding gums. She takes no new medicines. Her temperature is 37.1°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. She has scattered bruises on her arms and legs. Her platelets are 34 ×10⁹/L, haemoglobin 122 g/L and clotting is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her bruising?
questions.e: An isolated low platelet count with normal clotting in SLE is immune thrombocytopenia, one of the haematological features of lupus.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
**Isolated thrombocytopenia** with normal clotting in SLE.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Immune thrombocytopenia from SLE.

elim: Clotting would be deranged; hers is normal.
Inherited, usually in males, with prolonged APTT.
Needs haemolytic anaemia, fever, renal and neurological features.
Prolongs PT with a normal platelet count.

steps.x: **C. Immune thrombocytopenia from SLE.** SLE haematology: lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia, AIHA, low C3/C4.

questions.stem: A 37 year old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has severe, persistent joint and skin disease despite hydroxychloroquine. She stopped azathioprine because of abnormal liver tests. She has needed four courses of prednisolone this year and has gained 9 kg. Her urine dipstick is negative and there is no neurological involvement. Her BP is 126/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate steroid-sparing agent?
o: Increase hydroxychloroquine above the maximum dose
questions.e: Methotrexate is used as a steroid-sparing agent in severe SLE with prominent joint and skin involvement; cyclophosphamide is kept for organ-threatening flares.

steps.x: It asks for a management step: decide how unwell the patient is and what comes first.
Severe joint and skin disease, needing **repeated steroids**, azathioprine failed, **no organ-threatening** disease.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Methotrexate.

elim: Reserved for serious renal, neurological or haematological flares.
Raises the risk of retinal toxicity.
An anti-TNF used in rheumatoid arthritis and IBD, not standard in SLE.
She already has steroid side effects; the aim is to spare steroids.

steps.x: **E. Methotrexate.** Steroid-sparing in severe non-renal SLE: methotrexate.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus is followed in a combined lupus-renal clinic. Her urine dipstick has been clear for 2 years. The consultant wants to monitor the antibody that correlates best with disease activity and with risk of lupus nephritis.
questions.q: Which antibody is most appropriate to monitor?
questions.e: Anti-dsDNA is highly specific for SLE and its titre correlates with disease activity and lupus nephritis.

steps.x: It asks about a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.
Need an antibody whose **titre moves** with activity and the **kidneys**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Anti-dsDNA.

elim: Marker of drug-induced lupus, which spares the kidneys.
Linked to neonatal lupus and Sjögren's, not nephritis activity.
Highly specific but does not track disease activity or nephritis.
Stays positive regardless of activity; used to rule out.

steps.x: **A. Anti-dsDNA.** Anti-dsDNA: specific, tracks activity and nephritis.
